claim: C. elegans has a nervous system consisting of 302 neurons.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, with its small nervous system consisting of just 302 neurons, is ideally suited for a circuit-level analysis of chemosensory processing and behavior.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as established knowledge about C. elegans anatomy.

claim: Chemosensory stimuli in C. elegans are detected by twelve sensory neuron pairs located in the amphid ganglia.
source: Chemosensory stimuli are detected by twelve sensory neuron pairs located in the amphid ganglia (Figure 1A) (White et al., 1986; Bargmann, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and reference to Figure 1A showing the anatomical location.

claim: All 24 amphid sensory neurons send their dendrites to the nose of the animal where they detect environmental changes.
source: All 24 of these neurons send their dendrites to the nose of the animal where they detect environmental changes and relay that information through their axons to the downstream circuitry (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 1986, which describes the C. elegans connectome.

claim: AWC sensory neurons are necessary for attraction to benzaldehyde odor.
source: For example, single cell ablation experiments showed that the bilaterally asymmetric pair of AWC sensory neurons is necessary for attraction to benzaldehyde (BZ) odor, while the AWA sensory neuron pair is required for diacetyl odor attraction (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991; Bargmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior ablation studies.

claim: AWA sensory neurons are required for diacetyl odor attraction.
source: For example, single cell ablation experiments showed that the bilaterally asymmetric pair of AWC sensory neurons is necessary for attraction to benzaldehyde (BZ) odor, while the AWA sensory neuron pair is required for diacetyl odor attraction (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991; Bargmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior ablation studies.

claim: AWC neurons are activated by the removal of odor stimuli.
source: Functional imaging experiments revealed that AWC neurons are activated by the removal of odor stimuli (Chalasani et al., 2007), while AWA neurons respond to the addition of odors (Zaslaver et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior functional imaging work.

claim: AWA neurons respond to the addition of odors.
source: Functional imaging experiments revealed that AWC neurons are activated by the removal of odor stimuli (Chalasani et al., 2007), while AWA neurons respond to the addition of odors (Zaslaver et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior functional imaging work.

claim: AWCON neurons show a large calcium transient upon removal of medium concentration BZ stimulus in young adults.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we observed a large calcium transient indicating increased AWC activity upon removal of a medium concentration BZ stimulus (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) (Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures and consistent with prior citation.

claim: AWA neurons are activated by the addition of BZ in young adults.
source: Unexpectedly, we found additional BZ responsive neurons: the diacetyl sensing AWA neurons (Bargmann et al., 1993) were activated by the addition of BZ, while ASE and AWB neurons (that were previously shown to sense salts [Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991] and volatile repellents [Troemel et al., 1997; Bargmann, 2006], respectively) also responded to the removal of this stimulus in young adults (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a novel finding supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: ASE neurons respond to the removal of BZ stimulus in young adults.
source: Unexpectedly, we found additional BZ responsive neurons: the diacetyl sensing AWA neurons (Bargmann et al., 1993) were activated by the addition of BZ, while ASE and AWB neurons (that were previously shown to sense salts [Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991] and volatile repellents [Troemel et al., 1997; Bargmann, 2006], respectively) also responded to the removal of this stimulus in young adults (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a novel finding supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: AWB neurons respond to the removal of BZ stimulus in young adults.
source: Unexpectedly, we found additional BZ responsive neurons: the diacetyl sensing AWA neurons (Bargmann et al., 1993) were activated by the addition of BZ, while ASE and AWB neurons (that were previously shown to sense salts [Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991] and volatile repellents [Troemel et al., 1997; Bargmann, 2006], respectively) also responded to the removal of this stimulus in young adults (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a novel finding supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: ASE neurons were previously shown to sense salts.
source: Unexpectedly, we found additional BZ responsive neurons: the diacetyl sensing AWA neurons (Bargmann et al., 1993) were activated by the addition of BZ, while ASE and AWB neurons (that were previously shown to sense salts [Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991] and volatile repellents [Troemel et al., 1997; Bargmann, 2006], respectively) also responded to the removal of this stimulus in young adults (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on ASE neuron function.

claim: AWB neurons were previously shown to sense volatile repellents.
source: Unexpectedly, we found additional BZ responsive neurons: the diacetyl sensing AWA neurons (Bargmann et al., 1993) were activated by the addition of BZ, while ASE and AWB neurons (that were previously shown to sense salts [Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991] and volatile repellents [Troemel et al., 1997; Bargmann, 2006], respectively) also responded to the removal of this stimulus in young adults (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on AWB neuron function.

claim: None of the other amphid neurons responded to medium concentration BZ stimulus in young adults.
source: Furthermore, none of the other amphid neurons responded to this medium concentration BZ stimulus (Figure 1B,C Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: ASEL responses to BZ are slower to reach maximum response (average of 5.46 s after stimulus change) than other odor responsive neurons (average 1-2 s after stimulus change).
source: We also noted that the ASEL responses to BZ were slower to reach the maximum response (average of 5.46 s after stimulus change) than the other odor responsive neurons (average 1–2 s after stimulus change), indicating that the kinetics of odor-evoked activity are different in different cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Different neural activity patterns distributed across AWC, ASE, AWA, AWB and ASH sensory neurons define active neural circuits for different concentrations of BZ.
source: Moreover, different neural activity patterns distributed across AWC, ASE, AWA, AWB and ASH sensory neurons defined active neural circuits for different concentrations (medium as well as high or low) of BZ (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Genetic ablation or blocking synaptic transmission in AWC, ASE, AWA or AWB neurons impairs chemotaxis to medium BZ.
source: We found that genetic ablation (Beverly et al., 2011; Yoshida et al., 2012) or blocking synaptic transmission (with tetanus toxin [Schiavo et al., 1992]) in any of the four AWC, ASE, AWA or AWB neurons impaired animals' chemotaxis to a point source of medium BZ (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: AWCON responses to BZ are not affected in animals with AWA, ASE or AWB neurons ablated.
source: We found that AWCON responses to BZ were not affected in animals with any of the other BZ responsive neuron pairs (AWA, ASE or AWB neurons) ablated, suggesting that AWCON neurons directly detect the odor stimulus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from cell ablation experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: AWCON neurons directly detect BZ and function as primary sensory neurons.
source: We found that AWCON responses to BZ were not affected in animals with any of the other BZ responsive neuron pairs (AWA, ASE or AWB neurons) ablated, suggesting that AWCON neurons directly detect the odor stimulus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the cell ablation experiments showing AWCON responses are independent of other BZ-responsive neurons.

claim: AWA responses to BZ are not affected in animals with ablated AWC, ASE or AWB neurons.
source: Similarly, AWA responses to BZ were not affected in animals with ablated AWC, ASE or AWB neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from cell ablation experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AWA neurons directly detect BZ and function as primary sensory neurons.
source: Similarly, AWA responses to BZ were not affected in animals with ablated AWC, ASE or AWB neurons (Figure 2B). These experiments suggest that AWCON and AWA neurons directly detect BZ and function as primary sensory neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell ablation experiments showing AWA responses are independent of other BZ-responsive neurons.

claim: ASEL responses to BZ are greatly reduced in animals with ablated AWC neurons.
source: In contrast, ASEL responses to BZ were greatly reduced in animals with ablated AWC neurons, but unaffected by AWA or AWB neuron ablation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from cell ablation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ASEL responses to BZ are unaffected by AWA or AWB neuron ablation.
source: In contrast, ASEL responses to BZ were greatly reduced in animals with ablated AWC neurons, but unaffected by AWA or AWB neuron ablation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from cell ablation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ASEL neurons respond to signals from AWCON primary sensory neurons.
source: This suggests that ASEL neurons may respond to signals from AWCON primary sensory neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the cell ablation experiments showing ASEL responses depend on AWC neurons.

claim: AWB responses to BZ require signaling from AWA neurons.
source: Similarly, AWB responses to BZ required signaling from AWA neurons as these responses were significantly reduced specifically in the AWA ablation condition (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from cell ablation experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: AWB neurons may be inhibited by AWA neurons.
source: Interestingly, while AWA neurons responded to the addition of odor stimulus with an increase in the calcium signal, the AWB neuron calcium signal increased upon odor removal (Figure 2B,D). We suggest that AWB neurons may be inhibited by AWA and, when odor is removed, AWA is no longer active, leading to a release from inhibition and an increase in AWB activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the opposing temporal dynamics of AWA and AWB responses.

claim: The BZ olfactory circuit is composed of two primary sensory neurons (AWCON and AWA) and two secondary neurons (ASEL and AWB).
source: Collectively, these data show a novel sensory circuit configuration in which the odor responsive neurons are not equal: the olfactory circuit for BZ odor is composed of two primary sensory neurons (AWCON and AWA) and two secondary neurons (ASEL and AWB) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a synthesis of the cell ablation experiments defining the circuit architecture.

claim: AWCON and AWA neurons retain their odor responsiveness in the absence of classical or peptidergic neurotransmission.
source: We found that AWCON and AWA neurons retained their odor responsiveness in the absence of classical or peptidergic neurotransmission (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-13 and unc-31 mutants shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: AWCOFF responses to BZ are significantly reduced in unc-13 mutants.
source: Interestingly, we found that AWCOFF responses to BZ were significantly reduced in unc-13 mutants, suggesting that classical neurotransmission might be required to potentiate odor-evoked activity in this neuron (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-13 mutants shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Classical neurotransmission might be required to potentiate odor-evoked activity in AWCOFF neurons.
source: Interestingly, we found that AWCOFF responses to BZ were significantly reduced in unc-13 mutants, suggesting that classical neurotransmission might be required to potentiate odor-evoked activity in this neuron (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the reduced AWCOFF responses in unc-13 mutants.

claim: AWCOFF responses to BZ might be potentiated by classical neurotransmission from AWCON neuron.
source: We suggest that AWCOFF responses to BZ might be potentiated by classical neurotransmission from AWCON neuron.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying AWCOFF response reduction in unc-13 mutants.

claim: Odor-evoked ASEL activity requires unc-31-dependent neuropeptide signaling.
source: Specifically, odor-evoked ASEL activity required unc-31-dependent neuropeptide signaling (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-31 mutants shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Restoring neuropeptide release function specifically to AWC neurons rescues ASEL BZ responses in unc-31 mutants.
source: Restoring neuropeptide release function specifically to the AWC neurons rescued ASEL BZ responses in unc-31 mutants, suggesting that AWC neurons release peptides to recruit ASEL neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-31 mutants with AWC-specific rescue shown in Figure 3C.

claim: AWC neurons release peptides to recruit ASEL neurons.
source: Restoring neuropeptide release function specifically to the AWC neurons rescued ASEL BZ responses in unc-31 mutants, suggesting that AWC neurons release peptides to recruit ASEL neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing AWC-specific restoration of neuropeptide release rescues ASEL responses.

claim: The longer time required for ASEL neurons to reach their maximum response to odor may reflect the additional requirement of AWC-dependent peptidergic transmission.
source: This gene mutant analysis suggests that the longer time required for ASEL neurons to reach their maximum response to odor may reflect the additional requirement of AWC-dependent peptidergic transmission (Figure 3C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the kinetic differences in ASEL responses based on the neuropeptide signaling requirement.

claim: ASER responses to BZ require neuropeptide signaling.
source: Similarly, ASER responses to BZ also require neuropeptide signaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-31 mutants shown in the referenced figure.

claim: unc-13-dependent classical neurotransmission is not required for ASEL or ASER responses to BZ.
source: Moreover, unc-13-dependent classical neurotransmission was not required for either ASEL or ASER responses to BZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-13 mutants shown in the referenced figures.

claim: AWB responses to BZ are significantly reduced in unc-13 mutants.
source: AWB responses were significantly and specifically reduced in unc-13 mutants, suggesting that these neurons are recruited to this olfactory circuit by classical neurotransmitter(s) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-13 mutants shown in the referenced figures.

claim: AWB neurons are recruited to the olfactory circuit by classical neurotransmitter(s).
source: AWB responses were significantly and specifically reduced in unc-13 mutants, suggesting that these neurons are recruited to this olfactory circuit by classical neurotransmitter(s) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced AWB responses in unc-13 mutants which block classical neurotransmitter release.

claim: Expressing tetanus toxin specifically in AWA neurons significantly reduces AWB responses to BZ removal.
source: We found that expressing tetanus toxin specifically in the AWA, but not AWC, sensory neurons significantly reduced AWB responses to BZ removal (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in animals expressing tetanus toxin shown in Figure 3D.

claim: AWA signals to AWB and recruits it into the odor circuit.
source: This confirms that AWA signals to AWB and recruits it into the odor circuit.
evidence: This is inferred from the tetanus toxin experiments showing AWA-specific blockade reduces AWB responses.

claim: The insulin-like peptide ins-1 is required for BZ-evoked ASEL responses.
source: We found that the insulin-like peptide ins-1 (Pierce et al., 2001) was required for BZ-evoked ASEL responses (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in ins-1 mutants shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Restoring INS-1 function specifically to AWC neurons rescues mutant ASEL activity deficits.
source: Moreover, restoring INS-1 function specifically to AWC neurons, but not to AWA neurons, rescued mutant ASEL activity deficits (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in ins-1 mutants with AWC-specific rescue shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AWC neurons release INS-1 peptides to recruit ASEL neurons into the odor circuit.
source: This suggests that AWC neurons release INS-1 peptides to recruit ASEL neurons into the odor circuit.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing AWC-specific restoration of INS-1 rescues ASEL responses.

claim: Knocking down ins-1 in AWC neurons significantly reduces ASEL responses to BZ.
source: We found that knocking down ins-1 in AWC neurons significantly reduced the ASEL responses to BZ, confirming that AWC-released INS-1 is required for ASEL activity in the odor circuit (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in AWC-specific ins-1 RNAi animals shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AWC-released INS-1 is required for ASEL activity in the odor circuit.
source: We found that knocking down ins-1 in AWC neurons significantly reduced the ASEL responses to BZ, confirming that AWC-released INS-1 is required for ASEL activity in the odor circuit (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is confirmed by the AWC-specific ins-1 RNAi experiment showing reduced ASEL responses.

claim: INS-1 released from AIA interneurons inhibits AWC and ASER activity.
source: For example, INS-1 released from AIA interneurons inhibits AWC and ASER activity (Tomioka et al., 2006; Chalasani et al., 2010), while we show that INS-1 released from AWC recruits ASEL into the BZ circuit.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on INS-1 function in different cellular contexts.

claim: Odor-evoked ASEL activity requires the canonical insulin receptor (daf-2) signaling in ASEL neurons.
source: We found that odor-evoked ASEL activity required the canonical insulin receptor (daf-2 in C. elegans [Pierce et al., 2001]) and PI3-Kinase (age-1 in C. elegans [Morris et al., 1996]) signaling in ASEL neurons (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in daf-2 mutants with ASEL-specific rescue shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Odor-evoked ASEL activity requires PI3-Kinase (age-1) signaling in ASEL neurons.
source: We found that odor-evoked ASEL activity required the canonical insulin receptor (daf-2 in C. elegans [Pierce et al., 2001]) and PI3-Kinase (age-1 in C. elegans [Morris et al., 1996]) signaling in ASEL neurons (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in age-1 mutants with ASEL-specific rescue shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The increase in calcium in ASEL may result from rapid signaling downstream of PI3-Kinase acting directly on calcium channels.
source: We suggest that the increase in calcium in ASEL may result from rapid signaling downstream of PI3-Kinase acting directly on calcium channels (Blair and Marshall, 1997), and that this may represent an alternate pathway to the canonical, long term effects of DAF-2 signaling to regulate gene expression (Murphy et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying rapid ASEL calcium responses, supported by citation to prior work on PI3-Kinase signaling.

claim: The insulin receptor mutant (daf-2) has a stronger reduction in ASEL activity compared to the insulin ligand mutant (ins-1) or the insulin ligand knockdown animals.
source: Furthermore, we found that the insulin receptor mutant (daf-2) had a stronger reduction in ASEL activity compared to the insulin ligand mutant (ins-1) or the insulin ligand knockdown animals (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of calcium imaging data across different mutants shown in the referenced figures.

claim: AWC neurons may co-release additional insulin peptides along with INS-1 to bind the insulin receptor on ASEL neurons.
source: These results suggest that AWC neurons may co-release additional insulin peptides along with INS-1 to bind the insulin receptor on ASEL neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the stronger phenotype in daf-2 mutants compared to ins-1 mutants.

claim: AWCON primary olfactory neuron dynamics are normal in all of the insulin pathway mutants analyzed.
source: Importantly, we also confirmed that AWCON primary olfactory neuron dynamics were normal in all of the insulin pathway mutants analyzed, indicating that insulin signaling functions downstream of primary olfactory sensory transduction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in insulin pathway mutants shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Insulin signaling functions downstream of primary olfactory sensory transduction.
source: Importantly, we also confirmed that AWCON primary olfactory neuron dynamics were normal in all of the insulin pathway mutants analyzed, indicating that insulin signaling functions downstream of primary olfactory sensory transduction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is inferred from the normal AWCON responses in insulin pathway mutants.

claim: Primary ASEL responses to salt are not affected in daf-2 or age-1 mutants.
source: Furthermore, we have previously shown that ASEL responses to a different, directly detected stimulus, salt, are not affected in the daf-2 or age-1 mutants, suggesting that these primary ASEL responses do not depend on insulin signaling (Leinwand and Chalasani, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work showing context-dependent insulin signaling requirements.

claim: Mutations in the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (unc-17) reduce AWB odor responses.
source: We found that mutations in the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT), unc-17, which packs acetylcholine into synaptic vesicles (Alfonso et al., 1994), reduced AWB odor responses (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-17 mutants shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Restoring cholinergic function specifically in AWA primary neurons is sufficient to elicit wild-type-like activity in AWB secondary neurons.
source: Restoring cholinergic function specifically in AWA primary neurons was sufficient to elicit wild-type-like activity in AWB secondary neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-17 mutants with AWA-specific rescue shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Knocking down the choline acetyltransferase (cha-1) specifically in AWA neurons significantly reduces AWB neuron responses to BZ.
source: We found that knocking down the C. elegans choline acetyltransferase (ChaT), cha-1, which is required for the biosynthesis of acetylcholine (Rand and Russell, 1984; Alfonso et al., 1994), specifically in the AWA neurons significantly reduced AWB neuron responses to BZ (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in AWA-specific cha-1 RNAi animals shown in Figure 4F.

claim: AWA neuron-specific knockdown of the choline transporter cho-1 has no effect on AWB responses to BZ.
source: Interestingly, AWA neuron-specific knockdown of the choline transporter cho-1, which is required for high affinity choline reuptake at presynaptic terminals (Okuda et al., 2000), had no effect on AWB responses to BZ (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in AWA-specific cho-1 RNAi animals shown in Figure 4F.

claim: AWA requires the choline acetyltransferase, but may not require the high affinity choline transporter to release acetylcholine.
source: Therefore, we suggest that AWA requires the choline acetyltransferase, but may not require the high affinity choline transporter to release acetylcholine.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of cha-1 and cho-1 knockdown on AWB responses.

claim: Odor-evoked AWB activity is not affected in mutants of any of the three identified C. elegans muscarinic receptors (gar-1, gar-2 and gar-3).
source: We considered whether acetylcholine modulates AWB activity by acting on muscarinic receptors. We found that odor-evoked AWB activity was not affected in mutants of any of the three identified C. elegans muscarinic receptors (gar-1, gar-2 and gar-3) (data not shown), suggesting that acetylcholine might bind other receptors on AWB neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (not shown) testing muscarinic receptor mutants.

claim: Acetylcholine might bind receptors other than muscarinic receptors on AWB neurons.
source: We found that odor-evoked AWB activity was not affected in mutants of any of the three identified C. elegans muscarinic receptors (gar-1, gar-2 and gar-3) (data not shown), suggesting that acetylcholine might bind other receptors on AWB neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the lack of effect of muscarinic receptor mutations.

claim: AWA-released acetylcholine binds one of the C. elegans acetylcholine-gated chloride channels to inhibit AWB neuronal activity when odor is added.
source: The C. elegans genome encodes 8 acetylcholine-gated chloride channels (Hobert, 2013) and we suggest that AWA-released acetylcholine binds one of these receptors to inhibit AWB neuronal activity when odor is added, leading to a rebound from this inhibition when odor is removed.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying AWB inhibition by AWA, based on known receptor types.

claim: AWB responses to the directly detected repulsive odorant 2-nonanone are normal in unc-17 mutants.
source: Moreover, we found that AWB responses to the directly detected repulsive odorant 2-nonanone (Troemel et al., 1997) were normal in unc-17 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in unc-17 mutants shown in the referenced figure.

claim: AWB secondary (to BZ), but not primary (to 2-nonanone) responses require cholinergic signaling.
source: We suggest that AWB secondary (to BZ), but not primary (to 2-nonanone) responses require cholinergic signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of unc-17 mutation on AWB responses to BZ versus 2-nonanone.

claim: AWA primary olfactory neuron dynamics are normal in the genetic mutants and knockdown animals analyzed.
source: Importantly, we also confirmed that AWA primary olfactory neuron dynamics were normal in the genetic mutants and knockdown animals analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in cholinergic pathway mutants shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Knocking down the insulin-like peptide ins-1 in AWC neurons significantly reduces attraction to BZ.
source: Consistent with our imaging results, we found that knocking down the insulin-like peptide ins-1 in AWC neurons significantly reduced attraction to BZ (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data in AWC-specific ins-1 RNAi animals shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Animals with the choline acetyltransferase cha-1 knocked down specifically in AWA neurons display significantly reduced BZ chemotaxis behavior.
source: In addition, animals with the choline acetyltransferase cha-1 knocked down specifically in AWA neurons also displayed significantly reduced BZ chemotaxis behavior (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data in AWA-specific cha-1 RNAi animals shown in Figure 4H.

claim: BZ stimulus is encoded by AWCON and AWA primary sensory neurons, which use insulin peptidergic and cholinergic neurotransmission to elicit activity in ASEL and AWB secondary neurons and to shape chemotaxis behavior.
source: Together, these data show that BZ stimulus is encoded by AWCON and AWA primary sensory neurons, which use insulin peptidergic and cholinergic neurotransmission to elicit activity in ASEL and AWB secondary neurons and to shape chemotaxis behavior (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a synthesis of the neurotransmitter pathway mapping and behavioral experiments.

claim: Olfactory behavioral performance degrades with age.
source: Interestingly, olfactory behavioral performance has been previously shown to degrade with age, which in turn affects quality of life and overall safety and survival across species (Doty and Kamath, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on aging-associated olfactory decline.

claim: Young adults are strongly attracted to BZ odor, while older animals (day 4-6) show significant impairment in their attraction.
source: While young adults were strongly attracted to BZ odor, we found that older animals (day 4–6) showed a significant impairment in their attraction (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data across different ages shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The aging-associated chemotaxis behavioral deficit is unlikely to be caused by changes in locomotory ability.
source: Importantly, we found that the aging-associated chemotaxis behavioral deficit is unlikely to be caused by changes in locomotory ability since the speed of chemotaxing aged animals did not differ from that of young adults (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by speed analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Aging does not affect the reliability, duration or magnitude of odor-evoked activity in AWCON and AWA primary neurons.
source: Overall, aging did not affect the reliability, duration or magnitude of odor-evoked activity in AWCON and AWA primary neurons (Figure 5C,D,G–I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing young and aged animals shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Odor-evoked ASEL and AWB secondary neuron activity is highly variable with aging, with many neurons failing to show any responses to odor.
source: In contrast, odor-evoked ASEL and AWB secondary neuron activity was highly variable with aging, with many neurons failing to show any responses to odor, revealing a possible mechanism for behavioral decline (Figure 5E–I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing young and aged animals shown in the referenced figures.

claim: AWB neurons that respond to odor in aged animals have calcium transients that are indistinguishable from responses in younger animals.
source: Interestingly, the AWB neurons that did respond to odor in aged animals had calcium transients that were indistinguishable from responses in younger animals (Figure 5F–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Considering only the animals with odor responsive ASEL neurons, the BZ responses of the aged animals are significantly larger than that of the young animals.
source: Additionally, considering only the animals with odor responsive ASEL neurons, the BZ responses of the aged animals were in fact significantly larger than that of the young animals (Figure 5E,G,H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Odor-evoked activity in ASEL and AWB secondary neurons selectively decays in some animals.
source: These results suggest that odor-evoked activity in ASEL and AWB secondary neurons selectively decays in some animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the variability in aged secondary neuron responses.

claim: Aged animals that failed to chemotax towards BZ are significantly more likely to have odor non-responsive ASEL and AWB neurons than aged animals that successfully found the odor source.
source: We found that aged animals that failed to chemotax towards BZ were significantly more likely to have odor non-responsive ASEL and AWB neurons than aged animals that successfully found the odor source (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by correlated behavioral and calcium imaging data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: BZ behavioral declines arise from unreliable activity of aged secondary ASEL and AWB neurons.
source: Taken together, these data reveal a distributed neural circuit that detects attractive odors and suggest that BZ behavioral declines arise from unreliable activity of aged secondary ASEL and AWB neurons in this circuit.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the aging-related neural activity and behavioral data.

claim: High BZ is similarly repulsive in young and aged animals (through day 5).
source: Behaviorally, we found that high BZ was similarly repulsive in young and aged animals (through day 5) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data to high BZ shown in the referenced figure.

claim: High BZ-evoked neural activity does not significantly decline between day 1 and day 5 adults.
source: Consistently, high BZ-evoked neural activity did not significantly decline between day 1 and day 5 adults (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data to high BZ shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The aging-associated decline in neuronal function is dependent on odor concentration.
source: These data suggest that the aging-associated decline in neuronal function is dependent on odor concentration; consistent with previous studies showing relatively preserved behavioral detection of strong sensory stimuli with age (Hummel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of aging on responses to medium versus high BZ concentrations, and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neuronal activity and behavior in response to salt and 2-nonanone remain reliable and robust in aged animals.
source: We found that neuronal activity and behavior in response to these stimuli remained reliable and robust in aged animals (Figure 5K,L, Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging and behavioral data to salt and 2-nonanone shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Functionality of both ASEL and AWB neurons in aged animals is sensory context dependent.
source: These data indicate that functionality of both ASEL and AWB neurons in aged animals is sensory context dependent. Specifically, their primary responses to salt (ASEL) and 2-nonanone (AWB) are preserved, while their function as secondary neurons in encoding attractive BZ stimuli is impaired during aging.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of aging on primary versus secondary responses in ASEL and AWB neurons.

claim: AWC responses to salt are not reduced in aged animals.
source: However, we found that AWC responses to salt were not reduced in aged animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data to salt shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Early aging-associated deficits are specific to the BZ circuit, leaving the salt circuit fully functional.
source: These data suggest that these early aging-associated deficits are specific to the BZ circuit, leaving the salt circuit fully functional.
evidence: This is inferred from the preserved AWC secondary responses to salt in aged animals.

claim: ASEL and AWB secondary neuron responses to BZ in aged day 5 adults in wild-type, long-lived aak-2 (gf) and glp-1 mutants and rab-10 knockdown animals are unreliable.
source: We recorded ASEL and AWB secondary neuron responses to BZ in aged day 5 adults in wild-type, long-lived aak-2 (gf) and glp-1 mutants and rab-10 knockdown animals. Similar to wild-type, the ASEL and AWB responses to medium BZ in aak-2 (gf) and glp-1 mutants and rab-10 knockdown animals were unreliable in day 5 adults (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in long-lived mutants shown in the referenced figure.

claim: glp-1 mutants display a similar aging-associated decline in attraction to BZ compared to wild-type animals.
source: We found that glp-1 mutants displayed a similar aging-associated decline in attraction to BZ compared to wild-type animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 5I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data in glp-1 mutants shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Signaling from the longevity-modulating germline, AMP kinase energy sensing and Rab GTPase pathways do not attenuate secondary neuronal activity and behavior declines.
source: These data show that signaling from the longevity-modulating germline, AMP kinase energy sensing and Rab GTPase pathways do not attenuate secondary neuronal activity and behavior declines.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of rescue of aging-associated deficits in long-lived mutants.

claim: Animals with hsf-1 knocked down have similarly unreliable day 5 aged ASEL and AWB secondary neuron responses to BZ compared to wild-type.
source: We found that animals with hsf-1 knocked down had similarly unreliable day 5 aged ASEL and AWB secondary neuron responses to BZ compared to wild-type (Figure 5—figure-supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in hsf-1 RNAi animals shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The aging-associated declines in olfactory neuronal functions are independent of many known longevity pathways (glp-1, aak-2, rab-10 and hsf-1).
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the aging-associated declines in olfactory neuronal functions are independent of many known longevity pathways (glp-1, aak-2, rab-10 and hsf-1).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of rescue of aging-associated deficits in various longevity pathway mutants.

claim: Overexpressing the DAF-2 insulin receptor specifically in ASEL neurons shows no change in the reliability of aged animals' odor-evoked ASEL activity compared to wild-type.
source: However, we found no change in the reliability of these aged animals' odor-evoked ASEL activity compared to wild-type (Figure 6B,C,F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in ASEL-specific daf-2 OE animals shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Receptor expression is not limiting in aged animals.
source: This result suggests that receptor expression is not limiting in these aged animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of rescue by DAF-2 overexpression in ASEL.

claim: ASEL BZ responses are significantly larger in young adult animals overexpressing DAF-2 in ASEL.
source: We confirmed that our ASEL-specific DAF-2 overexpression (OE) was functional by analyzing ASEL responses in young day 1 adults. We found that the ASEL BZ responses were significantly larger in young adult animals overexpressing DAF-2 in ASEL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B) confirming the efficacy of the transgene.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in young ASEL-specific daf-2 OE animals shown in the referenced figures.

claim: DAF-2 receptors in ASEL are not reduced during the aging process and signaling via these receptors does not limit olfactory circuit activity in aged animals.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that DAF-2 receptors in ASEL are not reduced during the aging process and signaling via these receptors does not limit olfactory circuit activity in aged animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of rescue by DAF-2 overexpression in aged ASEL despite functional transgene in young animals.

claim: Over-expressing the insulin-like neuropeptide INS-1 in AWC neurons improves the reliability of odor-evoked activity in aged ASEL neurons.
source: To test this, we over-expressed the insulin-like neuropeptide INS-1 in the AWC neurons (Figure 6A, right panel). This manipulation succeeded in improving the reliability of odor-evoked activity in aged ASEL neurons, suggesting that increased neuropeptide production, and consequently release, can rescue aging-associated deficits (Figure 6D,F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in AWC-specific ins-1 OE animals shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Increased neuropeptide production, and consequently release, can rescue aging-associated deficits.
source: This manipulation succeeded in improving the reliability of odor-evoked activity in aged ASEL neurons, suggesting that increased neuropeptide production, and consequently release, can rescue aging-associated deficits (Figure 6D,F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of aged ASEL responses by INS-1 overexpression in AWC.

claim: Overexpressing INS-1 does not have a significant effect on the behavior of aged (or young) adults to BZ.
source: We also tested whether INS-1 (OE) could rescue aging-induced behavioral decline. We found that overexpressing INS-1 did not have a significant effect on the behavior of aged (or young) adults to BZ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data in AWC-specific ins-1 OE animals shown in the referenced figure.

claim: While INS-1 (OE) can rescue the age-induced neural activity deficits, this is not sufficient to rescue aging-induced behavioral deficits.
source: Together, these results show that while INS-1 (OE) can rescue the age-induced neural activity deficits, this is not sufficient to rescue aging-induced behavioral deficits.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the neural activity and behavioral data in INS-1 OE animals.

claim: AWC-specific RNAi knockdown of Tomosyn (tom-1) results in significantly more reliable odor-evoked ASEL activity in aged animals.
source: To confirm a role for increased AWC neurotransmission in recruiting ASEL neurons, we also generated an AWC-specific RNAi knockdown of Tomosyn (tom-1 in C. elegans [Gracheva et al., 2007; Leinwand and Chalasani, 2013]), a syntaxin-interacting protein that normally acts as a brake on all neurotransmission, to increase neuropeptide and neurotransmitter release from AWC neurons (Figure 6A, right panel). This manipulation to increase release from AWC neurons resulted in significantly more reliable odor-evoked ASEL activity (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in AWC-specific tom-1 RNAi animals shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Increased neurotransmission from the primary olfactory neurons specifically rescues the aging-associated ASEL defects.
source: These manipulations did not significantly affect ASEL responses in young day 1 adults (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that increased neurotransmission from the primary olfactory neurons specifically rescues the aging-associated ASEL defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the age-specific rescue by increased AWC neurotransmission.

claim: In aged day 5 adults, AWC-specific tom-1 knockdown animals show a significant improvement over wild-type in their attraction to BZ.
source: We also tested whether increased neurotransmission from AWC could rescue the aging-associated decline in chemotaxis behavior. We found that in aged day 5 adults, AWC-specific tom-1 knockdown animals showed a significant improvement over wild-type in their attraction to BZ (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data in AWC-specific tom-1 RNAi animals shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The improvement in aged chemotaxis by AWC-specific tom-1 knockdown requires the presence of functional ASE neurons.
source: Moreover, this improvement required the presence of functional ASE neurons (che-1 mutants do not have functional ASE neurons [Uchida et al., 2003]) (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data in AWC-specific tom-1 RNAi; che-1 mutant animals shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Experimental manipulations to increase neurotransmission from AWC neurons rescue aging-induced decline in ASEL secondary neuron activity and animal behavior.
source: Taken together, these results show that experimental manipulations to increase neurotransmission from AWC neurons rescue aging-induced decline in ASEL secondary neuron activity and animal behavior.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the rescue experiments using INS-1 OE and tom-1 RNAi.

claim: Over-expressing the vesicular acetylcholine transporter UNC-17 specifically in AWA neurons significantly increases the reliability of aged AWB odor responses.
source: We over-expressed the vesicular acetylcholine transporter, UNC-17, specifically in AWA neurons (Figure 7A). OE of the vesicular acetylcholine transporter was previously shown to increase the quantity of acetylcholine packed into and released from synaptic vesicles (Song et al., 1997). We found that this manipulation significantly increased the reliability of aged AWB odor responses (Figure 7B,C,E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), further suggesting that increased signaling from the primary neurons can overcome aging-associated declines.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in AWA-specific unc-17 OE animals shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Acute arecoline treatment in aged animals significantly increases the probability of AWB odor responses.
source: Arecoline is a cholinergic agonist known to act presynaptically to stimulate synaptic vesicle fusion (Liu et al., 2013) (Figure 7A). Acute arecoline treatment in aged animals significantly increased the probability of AWB odor responses (Figure 7D,E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that a pharmacological approach to increase neurotransmission in aged animals can rejuvenate neuronal functions.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in arecoline-treated animals shown in the referenced figures.

claim: A pharmacological approach to increase neurotransmission in aged animals can rejuvenate neuronal functions.
source: Acute arecoline treatment in aged animals significantly increased the probability of AWB odor responses (Figure 7D,E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that a pharmacological approach to increase neurotransmission in aged animals can rejuvenate neuronal functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of aged AWB responses by arecoline treatment.

claim: Neither the UNC-17 OE nor acute arecoline have significant effects on AWB responses in day 1 adults.
source: Moreover, neither the UNC-17 OE nor acute arecoline had significant effects on AWB responses in day 1 adults (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C), confirming a specific role for increased neurotransmission in rescuing aged-associated AWB defects.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in young animals shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Aged animals overexpressing the UNC-17 vesicular acetylcholine transporter in AWA neurons are significantly more attracted to BZ compared to aged wild-type animals.
source: We also tested whether increased cholinergic transmission from the AWA neurons could rescue the aging-associated defects in behavioral attraction to BZ. We found that aged animals overexpressing the UNC-17 vesicular acetylcholine transporter in AWA neurons were significantly more attracted to BZ compared to aged wild-type animals (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data in AWA-specific unc-17 OE animals shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The increased attraction to BZ in aged AWA-specific unc-17 OE animals requires the secondary AWB neurons.
source: Moreover, this increased attraction required the secondary AWB neurons (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data in AWA-specific unc-17 OE animals with AWB ablation shown in Figure 7F.

claim: AWA-AWB neurotransmission plays a role in rescuing aging-associated decline in BZ attraction.
source: These data confirm a role for AWA-AWB neurotransmission in rescuing aging-associated decline in BZ attraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the AWB-dependent rescue of aged chemotaxis by AWA-specific unc-17 OE.

claim: Arecoline pharmacology impairs BZ chemotaxis in both young and aged animals.
source: We note that while arecoline pharmacology rescued aged AWB neuronal activity, this treatment impaired BZ chemotaxis in both young and aged animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral chemotaxis data in arecoline-treated animals shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The known effect of arecoline to increase spontaneous locomotion may be counterproductive to the directed locomotion required to chemotax up an odor gradient.
source: We suggest that the known effect of arecoline to increase spontaneous locomotion may be counterproductive to the directed locomotion required to chemotax up an odor gradient (Glenn et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral impairment by arecoline, supported by citations to prior work on arecoline effects.

claim: Animals that successfully chemotaxed to the odor as aged adults have a significant extension (average of 16.2% in three separate trials) in lifespan compared to animals that failed to do so.
source: Notably, we observed a significant extension (average of 16.2% in three separate trials, p < 0.001, Mantel–Cox test) in the lifespan of animals that successfully chemotaxed to the odor as aged adults, compared to animals that failed to do so (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan analysis data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: There is no difference in the lifespan of animals that were sorted on the basis of their chemotaxis performance as young adults.
source: However, we found no difference in the lifespan of animals that were sorted on the basis of their chemotaxis performance as young adults (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan analysis data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The olfactory abilities of aged, but not young, animals may be correlated with their overall health, leading to lifespan differences.
source: These results suggest that the olfactory abilities of aged, but not young, animals may be correlated with their overall health, leading to lifespan differences.
evidence: This is inferred from the age-specific correlation between chemotaxis performance and lifespan.

claim: Sorting aged animals based on their attraction to salt does not result in any significant differences in lifespan.
source: In contrast, we found that sorting aged animals based on their attraction to salt did not result in any significant differences in lifespan (Figure 8—figure supplements 1,2A).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan analysis data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The increase in lifespan is likely to be specific to BZ and not the salt associated neural circuit.
source: These data show that the increase in lifespan is likely to be specific to BZ and not the salt associated neural circuit, consistent with the specific declines in BZ, not salt, evoked activity and behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of lifespan correlation with salt chemotaxis performance.

claim: The functionality of some, but not all, sensory neuronal circuits in early stage aged animals may predict animals' longevity.
source: Furthermore, these results indicate that the functionality of some, but not all, sensory neuronal circuits in early stage aged animals may predict animals' longevity.
evidence: This is inferred from the circuit-specific correlation between aged sensory function and lifespan.

claim: Loss of some chemosensory neurons affects C. elegans lifespan, while loss of other chemosensory neurons has no effect.
source: These data are also consistent with cell ablation experiments where loss of some chemosensory neurons affects C. elegans lifespan, while loss of other chemosensory neurons has no effect (Alcedo and Kenyon, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on chemosensory neuron ablation and lifespan.

claim: The olfactory prowess of aged animals is indicative of whole animal physiology, health and lifespan.
source: Together, these results suggest that the olfactory prowess of aged animals is indicative of whole animal physiology, health and lifespan.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the lifespan correlation data.

claim: Animals overexpressing the UNC-17 vesicular acetylcholine transporter in AWA neurons live an average of 26.6% longer than their wild-type counterparts (over three separate trials).
source: We found that animals overexpressing the UNC-17 vesicular acetylcholine transporter in AWA neurons lived an average of 26.6% longer than their wild-type counterparts (over three separate trials, p < 0.001, Mantel–Cox test) (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan analysis data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Increasing neurotransmission from AWC either by overexpressing the INS-1 peptide or by knocking down tom-1 results in a trend towards a small extension in lifespan.
source: Moreover, increasing neurotransmission from AWC either by overexpressing the INS-1 peptide or by knocking down tom-1, the C. elegans homolog of Tomosyn, resulted in a trend towards a small extension in lifespan (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan analysis data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Both classical neurotransmission (from AWA neurons) and neuropeptide signaling (from AWC neurons) may have a longevity promoting effect.
source: These data suggest that both classical neurotransmission (from AWA neurons) and neuropeptide signaling (from AWC neurons), which are key components of the combinatorial code for BZ, may have a longevity promoting effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the lifespan extension by increased neurotransmission from AWA and AWC.

claim: Animals expressing tetanus toxin in either AWA or AWC neurons to block their neurotransmission live significantly longer than wild-type (average of 36.0% and 27.6% longer, respectively, over two independent trials).
source: We analyzed the lifespan of animals in which AWA or AWC neurons were silenced rather than ablated. Animals expressing tetanus toxin in either AWA or AWC neurons to block their neurotransmission lived significantly longer than wild-type (average of 36.0% and 27.6% longer, respectively, over two independent trials, p < 0.01, Mantel–Cox test, Figure 8—figure supplement 2B,3).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan analysis data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: A balance in neurotransmission from the primary olfactory neurons is crucial to an animal's longevity; both higher than normal and lower than normal levels of neurotransmission extend lifespan.
source: Together, these results suggest that a balance in neurotransmission from the primary olfactory neurons is crucial to an animal's longevity; both higher than normal and lower than normal levels of neurotransmission extend lifespan.
evidence: This is inferred from the lifespan extension by both increased and decreased neurotransmission from AWA and AWC.

claim: Signaling from primary olfactory neurons is integrated by the downstream circuitry to mediate effects on the animal's lifespan.
source: We suggest that signaling from these primary olfactory neurons is integrated by the downstream circuitry to mediate effects on the animal's lifespan.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism linking olfactory neuron signaling to lifespan.

claim: C. elegans employ a combinatorial olfactory coding strategy as in flies and mice.
source: These data provide the first indication that C. elegans employ a combinatorial olfactory coding strategy as in flies and mice, suggesting that this strategy is essential for behavioral plasticity (Wang et al., 2003; Oka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the novel circuit architecture findings and supported by citations to prior work in other species.

claim: Combinatorial olfactory coding strategy is essential for behavioral plasticity.
source: These data provide the first indication that C. elegans employ a combinatorial olfactory coding strategy as in flies and mice, suggesting that this strategy is essential for behavioral plasticity (Wang et al., 2003; Oka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior work in other species.

claim: Primary olfactory neurons directly detect odors and use neurotransmission to recruit additional secondary neurons.
source: Moreover, we suggest that primary olfactory neurons directly detect odors and use neurotransmission to recruit additional secondary neurons.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the circuit architecture findings.

claim: Activity in the secondary neurons declines with aging, leading to behavioral deficits.
source: However, activity in the secondary neurons declines with aging, leading to behavioral deficits.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the aging-related neural activity and behavioral findings.

claim: The combination of primary and secondary neurons may be a common motif in sensory neural circuits from worms to mammals.
source: We propose that the combination of primary and secondary neurons may be a common motif in sensory neural circuits from worms to mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the circuit architecture findings.

claim: A distinct, but similarly distributed neural circuit (which does not include the ASE neurons) encodes a different attractive odorant, isoamyl alcohol.
source: A distinct, but similarly distributed neural circuit (which does not include the ASE neurons) encodes a different attractive odorant, isoamyl alcohol (data not shown, [Yoshida et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by unpublished data and citation to prior work.

claim: The C. elegans salt neural circuit is composed of a primary salt sensory neuron, ASEL, which releases INS-6 insulin neuropeptides to recruit a secondary sensory neuron, AWCON, into the circuit in particular sensory contexts.
source: Furthermore, we have previously shown that the C. elegans salt neural circuit is composed of a primary salt sensory neuron, ASEL, which releases INS-6 insulin neuropeptides to recruit a secondary sensory neuron, AWCON, into the circuit in particular sensory contexts (Leinwand and Chalasani, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Combined primary and secondary neuron coding strategy is likely to increase the signal-to-noise ratios, thus preventing failures in encoding sensory information.
source: This combined primary and secondary neuron coding strategy is likely to increase the signal-to-noise ratios, thus preventing failures in encoding sensory information.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional advantage of the circuit architecture.

claim: Combinatorial coding may be broadly useful for distinguishing different concentrations of the same stimulus, as they will be encoded by overlapping but distinct subsets of neurons.
source: Combinatorial coding of this sort may also be broadly useful for distinguishing different concentrations of the same stimulus, as they will be encoded by overlapping but distinct subsets of neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional advantage of the circuit architecture.

claim: The insulin peptidergic and cholinergic signaling from primary to secondary olfactory neurons could add salience to volatile food signals in a complex, multisensory environment.
source: Furthermore, the insulin peptidergic and cholinergic signaling from primary to secondary olfactory neurons could add salience to volatile food signals in a complex, multisensory environment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of the neurotransmitter pathways.

claim: Insulin and cholinergic receptors are expressed in mammalian olfactory processing centers.
source: Previous studies have shown that insulin (Lacroix et al., 2008) and cholinergic receptors (Ogura et al., 2011) are expressed in mammalian olfactory processing centers, suggesting that these signaling pathways might also be used to encode odors in mammals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on mammalian olfactory systems.

claim: Primary sensory transduction remains robust as animals age.
source: We find that primary sensory transduction remains robust as animals age.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the aging-related neural activity findings.

claim: The combinatorial code for attractive volatile cues degrades with age because the activity of cells functioning as secondary neurons decays with age.
source: However, the combinatorial code for attractive volatile cues degrades with age because the activity of cells functioning as secondary neurons decays with age.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the aging-related neural activity findings.

claim: Aging-induced decline in neuronal function is dependent on the interplay between sensory context and neuronal identity.
source: Our results show that aging-induced decline in neuronal function is dependent on the interplay between sensory context and neuronal identity.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the context-dependent aging effects on neural activity.

claim: Primary ASEL responses to salt and AWB responses to 2-nonanone are preserved while their secondary responses to BZ are reduced in aged animals.
source: For example, we find that primary ASEL responses to salt and AWB responses to 2-nonanone are preserved while their secondary responses to BZ are reduced in aged animals.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the context-dependent aging effects on neural activity.

claim: There is an early stage age-induced decline in the primary ASH neuron responses to hyperosmotic stimuli.
source: This is in contrast with studies showing an early stage age-induced decline in the primary ASH neuron responses to hyperosmotic stimuli (Chokshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on aging effects on ASH neurons.

claim: Aging differentially affects sensory circuits, perhaps reflecting differences in physiological demand and the importance of diverse sensory contexts as the animal ages.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that aging differentially affects sensory circuits, perhaps reflecting differences in physiological demand and the importance of diverse sensory contexts as the animal ages.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the circuit-specific aging effects.

claim: Aging-associated sensory declines occur independently of many known longevity pathways.
source: Furthermore, these aging-associated sensory declines occur independently of many known longevity pathways.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the longevity pathway mutant experiments.

claim: Insulin signaling is required for the primary AWCON to secondary ASEL neurotransmission.
source: We find that insulin signaling is required for the primary AWCON to secondary ASEL neurotransmission and so are unable to separate its longevity promoting effect from its role in encoding sensory information.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the insulin pathway mapping experiments.

claim: The insulin signaling pathway might affect both the quality of an animal's life by encoding odors based on sensory context and also its lifespan.
source: We speculate that the insulin signaling pathway might affect both the quality of an animal's life by encoding odors based on sensory context and also its lifespan.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the dual roles of insulin signaling.

claim: Experimental manipulations targeting neurotransmission pathways improve the aging-associated neuronal activity and olfactory behavioral declines.
source: Our experiments show that experimental manipulations targeting neurotransmission pathways improve the aging-associated neuronal activity and olfactory behavioral declines.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the rescue experiments.

claim: There is no aging-associated reduction in the expression of peptidergic and cholinergic genes at the whole animal level.
source: A decline in peptidergic and cholinergic gene expression with age could contribute; however, quantitative RT-PCR experiments suggest that there is no aging-associated reduction in the expression of these genes at the whole animal level [data not shown and (Jin et al., 2011)].
evidence: This is supported by unpublished data and citation to prior work.

claim: The early aging-associated sensory impairments are driven at least in part by reduced neurotransmitter release from primary neurons.
source: Nevertheless, we speculate that the early aging-associated sensory impairments are driven at least in part by reduced neurotransmitter release from primary neurons, a mechanism likely applicable across species.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying aging-associated deficits.

claim: Aging affects multiple steps in the neurotransmitter release pathway.
source: We find that both increasing neurotransmitter production and release capacity rescue the aging-associated deficits. Therefore, it is likely that aging affects multiple steps in the neurotransmitter release pathway, emphasizing the key role played by this machinery in regulating animal behavior and physiology.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue by multiple different manipulations of the neurotransmitter pathway.

claim: There is reduced synapse number in the aged mammalian olfactory bulb.
source: These results are consistent with reports of reduced synapse number in the aged mammalian olfactory bulb, which should disrupt olfactory circuits (Richard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on mammalian olfactory aging.

claim: Differences in synaptic transmission explain some of the inter-individual variability in aging phenotypes.
source: We speculate that these differences in synaptic transmission also explain some of the inter-individual variability in aging phenotypes (Pinto et al., 2014; Vijg, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior work on aging variability.

claim: Circuit-level changes in synaptic transmission could produce hyposmia or anosmia, which may be among the earliest predictors of lifespan and mortality across species.
source: Subsequently, these circuit-level changes could produce hyposmia or anosmia, which may be among the earliest predictors of lifespan and mortality across species (Toth et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013; Pinto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior work on olfactory function and mortality.

claim: Alterations in transmitter release, which disrupt neuronal communication throughout the brain, are likely to underlie variability in individual animal behavior and age-related cognitive and behavioral decline.
source: More generally, we suggest that alterations in transmitter release, which disrupt neuronal communication throughout the brain (Dickstein et al., 2007) are likely to underlie variability in individual animal behavior and age-related cognitive and behavioral decline.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to prior work on neurotransmitter release and brain function.
